Exam skills for any English test: catching details, spotting paraphrases, typing what you hear, and speaking with a clear structure.

01

Five exam habits.

Keep these in mind for every task today. We'll come back to them after each one.

Habit 1

Read first.

Look at the questions before the audio starts and predict the type of answer: a number, a name, a noun?

Habit 2

Expect synonyms.

The answer is usually said in different words from the question.

Habit 3

Wait for the change.

"Sorry", "actually", "no, wait": the first thing you hear is often wrong.

Habit 4

Check the small stuff.

Spelling, plurals, numbers and capital letters can cost points.

Habit 5

Structure beats perfect.

Start, develop, finish. A clear plan makes your speaking sound fluent.

02

New city, new chapter.

Answer in two or three sentences. Give a reason or an example every time.

  1. You moved from Krasnodar to Moscow. What surprised you the most?
  2. How would you explain what a creative events manager does to someone who has never heard of the job?
  3. If you could take any course in English at your university, what would it be and why?
  4. What makes an event memorable for you: the people, the place, or the idea?
  5. Which English exam skill feels hardest for you right now, and why?

04

Booking the venue.

A student calls an arts space to book a room for a design exhibition. Read the form first. Then write one word or a number in each gap.

  • fifty guests → ninety
  • Gallery Room → Glass Hall
  • £400 → £320 with the student discount
  • Saturday 14th → Sunday 15th
  • frames → a projector
  • 11 a.m. doors open → set up before 9

05

Same idea, different words.

An event producer talks about a magic-themed night for first-year students. The right answer rarely uses the words you hear.

06

Type what you hear.

University-style sentences. Listen, type the whole sentence, then check. Small words like a, the and has been count too.

07

Listen, then answer.

Opinion questions like the ones in speaking exams. Play one, then answer for about 45 seconds: give your view, a reason and an example. The text stays hidden until you finish.

0:45
08

Thirty to think, sixty to talk.

Pick a card. Plan for 30 seconds, then speak for a full minute.

Start

I'd like to talk about…
The first thing that comes to mind is…

Develop

What I find most interesting is…
To give you an example, …
On top of that, …

Finish

That's the main reason why…
If I had to sum it up, …

Discuss

It depends on…
On the one hand… on the other…
0:30Ready
Card A

An artist who influenced you

Who are they? How did you discover their work? Why do they still matter to you?

Then discuss: Can music or art change the way people think?

Card B

An event you'd love to organise

What would it be? Who is it for? Where would it happen? What would make it memorable?

Then discuss: Are big events worth the money they cost?

Card C

A story you loved growing up

A book or film series from your childhood. What was special about it? Does it mean the same to you now?

Then discuss: Why do some stories stay popular for decades?
